name: Yuan China
title: Social Hierarchy of Yuan China: From Great Khan to the Enslaved
period: 1271–1368 (from Kublai Khan's proclamation of the Great Yuan to the fall of the dynasty)

tiers.name: The emperor and Great Khan
tiers.you: You are Great Khan to the Mongols and emperor to the Chinese, elected by an assembly of princes, but no law fixes the succession, and empress dowagers, guards and ministers will make your successors.
tiers.kid: The Yuan ruler was called the Great Khan by the Mongols and the emperor by the Chinese.
tiers.rise: Any descendant of Kublai could rule, chosen by an assembly of princes or, later, by whichever faction held the guards and the capital. The last emperor, Toghon Temür, fled north to the steppe in 1368 as the Ming army approached.
tiers.why: The Yuan ruler was at once emperor (huangdi) to his Chinese subjects and khagan, Great Khan, to the Mongols.

tiers.name: Mongol princes and imperial in-laws
tiers.you: You descend from Genghis Khan, live on the revenue of an appanage of households and help choose the khagan, but a prince who rebels against him can be smothered under felt carpets.
tiers.kid: Mongol princes were relatives of the emperor who lived on the taxes of lands given to them.
tiers.rise: Only birth into the line of Genghis Khan made a prince, and only marriage made an in-law. A prince who rebelled or backed the losing claimant could lose his troops, his appanage and his life.
tiers.why: Below the emperor stood the Golden Lineage, the princes descended from Genghis Khan, and the families that married into it.

tiers.name: Officials
tiers.you: You serve as the Mongol or semu overseer of a district, a post closed to the Chinese, and you owe your office to a recommendation or to your father’s privilege rather than to an examination.
tiers.kid: Yuan officials ran the government, and the very top jobs were kept for Mongols and peoples from Central and West Asia.
tiers.rise: Most officials entered by recommendation, through their fathers’ privilege or through the School for the Sons of the State, founded in 1271 for the sons of the imperial guards. From 1315 a few won office by examination, and half of those places were reserved for Mongols and semu.
tiers.why: The Yuan kept the institutions of a Chinese state, a Central Secretariat, a Bureau of Military Affairs and a Censorate, but filled the posts by origin.

tiers.name: Clergy
tiers.term: dishi (Imperial Preceptor), xiansheng (Daoist masters), erke'üd (Christian clergy)
tiers.you: You are a monk, spared taxes and labour service under a decree that goes back to Genghis Khan; if you were a Tibetan lama, you would stand closest to the court.
tiers.kid: Buddhist monks, above all the lamas of Tibet, were honoured at the Yuan court and excused from many taxes.
tiers.rise: Men and women entered the clergy by taking vows, and service to the court could lead far: Sangha, who rose through the Buddhist bureau, became the dynasty’s chief fiscal officer in 1286. In 1329 foreign clerics, Muslims among them, lost their tax exemptions.
tiers.why: The Mongols honoured the holy men of every faith.

tiers.name: Confucian scholars
tiers.you: You are a scholar of the Confucian classics, but with no examinations to sit you earn your living as a teacher or a physician, or write for the stage; at least your household is spared labour service.
tiers.kid: With no government exams for many years, many Chinese scholars became teachers, doctors and writers.
tiers.rise: From 1315 a scholar could again win office by examination, though southerners competed for a quarter of the places. Others reached office by recommendation, as the scholar and painter Zhao Mengfu, a descendant of the Song emperors, did after Kublai received him in 1286.
tiers.why: The Confucian literati, who under the Song had filled the bureaucracy through the examinations, lost their road to power.

tiers.name: Merchants
tiers.you: You trade with silver entrusted to you by a Mongol prince, travel by the official post-stations and lend at high interest, and the Chinese officials around you resent your privileges.
tiers.kid: Some merchants were business partners of Mongol princes, who gave them silver to trade with.
tiers.rise: Trade could bring influence: in Quanzhou, Muslim merchant families combined commerce with political power. At the end of the dynasty their wealth drew a violent backlash from the Chinese.
tiers.why: Trade prospered under Mongol rule, and the richest merchants were partners of the rulers themselves.

tiers.name: Soldiers
tiers.term: tammachi, hanjun (Han army), xinfujun ("Newly Adhered" army)
tiers.you: Your household owes the army a soldier in every generation; as a Mongol settled in China you must buy your own horse, and the harvests of your Chinese tenants barely cover the cost of your equipment.
tiers.kid: Soldiers’ families had to send a man to the army in every generation.
tiers.rise: Service passed from father to son, and an officer’s command to his heir. Many Mongol households sank into poverty under its costs, and by 1290 some Mongol commoners were selling their children into slavery.
tiers.why: The Yuan drew its soldiers from hereditary military households, registered under the Bureau of Military Affairs, which had to supply men and their equipment generation after generation.

tiers.name: Northern Chinese
tiers.you: You farm the plains of the Yellow River, owe labour on the state’s river works and may not keep a weapon, but as one of the Han ren you rank above the southerners.
tiers.kid: Northern Chinese farmers ranked above the southern Chinese under Mongol rule.
tiers.rise: Northern Chinese could rise through the army, as the Han generals who fought for the Mongols did, or from 1315 through the examinations, where they had a quarter of the places. Famine and the state’s demands drove others from their land.
tiers.why: The third category, the Han ren, took in the subjects of the former Jin state in the north: northern Chinese, together with Khitans, Jurchens and Koreans.

tiers.name: Southern Chinese
tiers.you: You grow rice in the rich south, perhaps as a tenant of a great landlord, and pay your taxes under rulers who keep the highest offices closed to southerners like you.
tiers.kid: Southern Chinese were the biggest group in Yuan China but the least favoured by its Mongol rulers.
tiers.rise: Southerners were the least likely of all to reach office, though a few scholars won posts by recommendation or examination. Wealth from land and trade let some southern families prosper despite their low legal standing.
tiers.why: The southerners (nanren), the subjects of the Southern Song conquered in the 1270s, were by far the largest group and the lowest of the four, because they had resisted longest.

tiers.name: Enslaved people
tiers.you: You belong to the household of a Mongol commander, who took you captive when his army stormed your city, and your children will belong to him too.
tiers.kid: Enslaved people were owned by others and made to work without pay; many had been captured in wars.
tiers.rise: An owner could release a slave to live as a commoner; otherwise bondage passed to the slave’s children.
tiers.why: The Mongol conquests enslaved great numbers of people.
